Fully open-weight and European-trained, it empowers sovereign AI with customizable, self-hosted deployment options.

...

Today, we're releasing the weights of this improved Mistral Large 4. The new model also features substantial gains in reasoning efficiency that give developers greater performance while lowering inference costs.

...

Mistral Large 4 entered public preview with strong results across leading coding benchmarks. Just three weeks of additional reinforcement learning have since propelled it to the forefront of open-weight coding, taking the lead on FrontierCode and Terminal-Bench while matching the best open-weight models on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index with substantially greater token efficiency.

On Cognition's private FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark, which assesses end-to-end code quality and whether a repository maintainer would merge the agent's change, Mistral Large 4 leads with a score of 19.7%.

...

...

The gains extend to terminal-based coding workflows. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Mistral Large 4 improved by 13 percentage points to 41% compared to its public preview, taking the lead among open-weight models while reducing output tokens by 30%.

signals.title: 3 Ways to Boost MoE Inference on NVIDIA DGX Spark | NVIDIA Technical Blog
signals.excerpt:
- Ling-3.0-flash is a 124-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 5.1 billion active parameters per token, evaluated on NVIDIA DGX Spark at batch size 1.
- Profiling showed decoding was memory-bound, with the MoE computation and output-layer projection driving execution time.
- Replacing the FlashInfer MXFP4 MoE backend with the Humming kernel library reduced time per output token from 27.71 ms to 25.35 ms, a 9.3% throughput gain.
- Online FP8 quantization of the LM head halved its weight-read volume and, combined with Humming, improved decode throughput 21.7% over the baseline.
- Multi-token prediction speculative decoding using the model's built-in NEXTN layer achieved 3.90 accepted tokens per round on a synthetic workload, raising throughput 185.1% over the baseline.
- On the full GSM8K test set, the three optimizations together increased decode throughput 42.5% and reduced mean latency 24.5% with no statistically detectable accuracy change.

...

Generating tokens faster starts with identifying what limits inference performance. In the batch-size-1 evaluation of Ling-3.0-flash from Inclusion AI on NVIDIA DGX Spark, profiling showed that decoding was memory-bound: reading model weights drove execution time. Two operations stood out—the mixture-of-experts (MoE) computation and the output-layer projection that produces scores across the model’s vocabulary.

Those findings pointed to two ways to improve performance: reduce the weight traffic in each decode step and generate more tokens per verification round. This post examines three techniques that address those costs:

- Humming MXFP4 MoE kernels to improve execution of the routed-expert computation.
- Online FP8 quantization of the output layer, or LM head, to reduce its weight-read volume.
- Multi-token prediction (MTP) speculative decoding with NEXTN to draft and verify multiple tokens together.

...

## Optimization 2: Online FP8 LM head quantization

In the checkpoint, the LM head is stored in BF16 and listed in modules_to_not_convert, so it is not quantized during loading. Its vocabulary GEMM is 157,184 × 2,560, and the entire weight block must be read for each generated token. Under a bandwidth bottleneck, it is therefore a high-value target for compression.

The optimization applies a dynamic FP8 quantization configuration only when constructing the LM head. The rest of the model continues to load with the checkpoint’s FP8/MXFP4 configuration. Moving the LM-head weights from BF16 to FP8 halves the read volume for this layer. The configuration is enabled with SGLANG_ENABLE_FP8_LM_HEAD=1.

This setting is mutually exclusive with the baseline –enable-fp32-lm-head option, which outputs logits in FP32 and uses a slower vocabulary-GEMM path.

| Configuration | TPOT | Decode throughput | Relative to baseline |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Baseline | 27.71 ms | 36.09 tok/s | — |
| + Humming MoE backend | 25.35 ms | 39.45 tok/s | +9.3% |
| + Online FP8 LM head | 22.76 ms | 43.94 tok/s | +21.7% |

Table 2. Cumulative effects of Humming and online FP8 LM-head quantization on NVIDIA DGX Spark, using a synthetic workload with 32K input tokens, 2K output tokens, and batch size 1. Adding FP8 increases decode throughput by 11.4% over Humming alone

...

When online FP8 LM-head quantization and MTP are enabled together, the draft model must share the entire LM-head module with the target, rather than only its weight tensor. The original Ling NEXTN implementation didn’t expose this interface. Without it, the framework silently falls back: the draft receives FP8 weights but interprets them as BF16, accept length drops to 1.00, and throughput becomes lower than a configuration with no optimizations.

...

| Configuration | TPOT | Decode throughput | Relative to baseline |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Baseline | 27.71 ms | 36.09 tok/s | — |
| + Humming MoE backend | 25.35 ms | 39.45 tok/s | +9.3% |
| + Online FP8 LM head | 22.76 ms | 43.94 tok/s | +21.7% |
| + MTP (NEXTN, steps=3 / topk=1 / draft_tokens=4) | 9.72 ms | 102.88 tok/s | +185.1% |

...

Across the full GSM8K evaluation, the three optimizations increased decode throughput by 42.5%, reduced mean end-to-end latency by 24.5%, and produced no statistically detectable accuracy change. Their mechanisms do not overlap: Humming and the FP8 LM head reduce the cost of each step, while MTP reduces the number of steps, so the techniques can be combined.

Stacking, however, is not automatic. Each optimization worked independently, but enabling all three required the draft model to share the full LM-head module. Otherwise, the system silently degrades to a configuration slower than the unoptimized baseline. During deployment, validate that every optimization is active at startup; this is more reliable than inferring configuration state from later performance numbers.

signals.title: ViBench 2.0: A Long-Horizon Software Benchmark | Replit
signals.excerpt:
# ViBench 2.0: A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Software Building

Can agents build whole products one feature at a time?

Published:

Oct 28, 2026

Preeya Kirani

Daniel Furman

Peter Zhong

Michele Catasta

Today we’re releasing ViBench 2.0, a benchmark for long-horizon software development. It joins the Specialized Intelligence Index (SII) from Fireworks [1], our partner for open-weight model inference and training. The SII brings together practitioner-built benchmarks to compare open, closed, and specialized models on real work tasks across industries.

Most coding benchmarks, like DeepSWE [2], hand an agent a well-defined task inside an existing codebase. In ViBench 2.0, the agent starts with an empty project instead. It then builds a whole product one feature at a time, modeled on products like Uber, GitHub, or Google Docs.

ViBench 2.0 has seventeen products, 241 feature requests, and 544 test plans. The best models, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Opus 5.5, pass all test plans in only 49⁠-⁠65% of their builds.

...

The official ViBench 2.0 results come from Fireworks’ runs: four builds of the seventeen products per model, on the same harness and settings.

...

### ViBench 2.0: pass@1 against cost per build

Mean of 4 builds of each of 17 products. Whiskers are 95% intervals.

Pass@1 is the share of builds in which every test plan passes, averaged over four builds of each product.

GPT-6.1 Sol leads with a pass@1 of 65%, followed by GPT-6 Astra at 60% and Opus 5.5 at 49%. All three pass more than 90% of their test plans, so most of their failed builds miss by only a few plans. Sol costs about $12 per build, and Astra about $90. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash passes 77% of its test plans for about $2.50 per build, though no open-weight model passes a full build. Opus 5.5 finishes a build in about 70 minutes on average, roughly 2.5 times faster than Sol. Opus produces only about 6% fewer tokens, so the gap mostly comes from API provider speed.

signals.title: AI agents on a short leash: PipesHub searches company knowledge | heise online
signals.excerpt:
The first major release introduces, among other things, code graphs for repository analysis, tighter guardrails for AI tools and a revamped search pipeline.

...

PipesHub is an open-source, self-hosted alternative to commercial enterprise search services such as Glean. The system, developed on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license, is aimed at companies and development teams that want to make internal data sources searchable or provide them as context for large language models and AI agents without sending data to third-party cloud environments. The software connects to existing systems through more than 50 connectors and inherits their access permissions (permission-aware search). Anyone who isn’t allowed to see a document in Google Drive or a ticket in Jira also won’t receive information from it through PipesHub or connected AI assistants. The system includes citations in its answers, down to individual text passages.

Technically, the platform combines a vector database (Qdrant) for similarity searches with a graph database — Neo4j or ArangoDB by default — as well as MongoDB. With this knowledge graph approach, PipesHub captures not only similar text passages but also structural relationships between documents, users and systems. For language models, the project says on its website it follows a “Bring Your Own Model” approach: Administrators can connect APIs from providers such as OpenAI or Anthropic, or run local models through Ollama. External tools such as Claude Code or Cursor can access the knowledge context through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) or SDKs for Python, TypeScript and Go.

signals.title: PyTorch 2.15 Release Blog
signals.excerpt:
We are excited to announce the release of PyTorch® 2.15 (release notes)!

The PyTorch 2.15 release features the following changes:

- Rewritten NCCL backend becomes the default, with a flight recorder that dumps on hangs and `TORCH_DIST_USE_NCCL2=0` or `nccl-legacy` as rollback paths
- One-sided transports for torch.distributed, with a NIXL backend and CUDA-graph-capturable transfers
- **FSDP2 and pipelining gain finer memory and communication control,**with fp32 for precision-sensitive parameters, CUDA-graph-captured gradient accumulation, and gradient reduction overlapped with compute 
-   Faster 4-bit (NVFP4) LLM decoding on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs through fewer, better-overlapped kernel launches in NVGEMM
- Apple Silicon gains FP8 and faster decode, with `float8_e4m3fn` and `_scaled_mm`, a new grouped_mm with a decode fast path (1.32–1.34x tokens/s on MoE decode), and public `torch.mps.Stream` APIs
- Broader platform support with FlyDSL kernels on AMD gfx950, Tensor Data Mover support for gfx1250 (MI450), ROCm 10.0 wheels, simpler SYCL kernel authoring and multi-GPU profiling on Intel GPUs, CUDA 13.2 as the default wheel with CUDA 13.4 alongside it, and torch.compile on Python 3.15

...

PyTorch 2.15 builds on that work. The rewritten NCCL backend now backs every `nccl` process group, NVGEMM is tuned for low-precision decode, Apple Silicon adds FP8 and decode-specific kernels, AMD support extends to new compiler DSLs and (preview support) for next Instinct generation, and Intel GPUs gain a simpler kernel programming model and deeper profiling.

...

In PyTorch 2.15,

...

#### NVGEMM for NVFP4 Decode

NVGEMM, the CuTeDSL GEMM backend added in 2.14, now folds the scalar dequantization factor of ModelOpt NVFP4 linear layers into the GEMM, removing a separate pointwise launch per layer during decode. A bounded, shape-aware candidate policy covers Blackwell NVFP4 decode shapes that nvMatmulHeuristics misses, and NVGEMM kernels can use programmatic dependent launch so a Triton consumer overlaps with the tail of the producer GEMM. NVGEMM also moves onto CUTLASS Operators.

signals.title: Accelerate agentic AI with NVIDIA Nemotron models on Amazon EKS and SageMaker HyperPod EKS | Artificial Intelligence
signals.excerpt:
NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL joins the NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano, Nano Omni, Super, Ultra, and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning models already available on AWS. It’s a 120B-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model that activates 12B parameters per token. It combines reasoning and tool use with text, image, document, and video understanding, so one model serves both text and visual tasks. This post explores its architecture and use cases, then shows how to deploy it on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Amazon EKS Auto Mode, and Amazon SageMaker HyperPod EKS.

...

NVIDIA reports 63.44 percent on Hermes Bench and 87.05 percent on LangChain agent evaluations, and 80.8 percent on the CharXiv chart-reasoning benchmark. (technical report)

...

### Deployment architecture

The reference implementation runs on standard Amazon EKS, EKS Auto Mode, and SageMaker HyperPod EKS. With EKS Auto Mode, AWS manages scaling, GPU, and EFA support in the cluster on your behalf. The Kubernetes manifests for model deployment are the same for each of the orchestrator options. Each cluster has a control plane hosting the Kubernetes API and a data plane of CPU and GPU nodes. CPU nodes run system and test pods, while the GPU nodes run the model. Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) stores the container images, a shared Amazon FSx for Lustre volume holds the model weights, and Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) connects the GPU nodes. The following figure shows a standard Amazon EKS cluster.

...

This architecture has been validated on both p6-b200.48xlarge (8 x NVIDIA B200 GPUs) and p5en.48xlarge (8 x NVIDIA H200 GPUs) instances. You can validate the cluster and its network with an NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) all-reduce micro-benchmark.

...

You can measure the performance of a deployed model on the cluster with the NVIDIA aiperf tool.

...

The aiperf output in the upper left pane shows key performance indicators (KPIs) like time to first token (TTFT), inter-token latency (ITL), and throughput in tokens per second (TPS). By taking these measurements at various levels of concurrency, we can study how latency and throughput depend on the number of concurrent requests. This information is essential to thoughtfully plan capacity and model deployment topology. The aws-do-eks container provides automation for visualizing GPU and EFA utilization as well as running aiperf and concurrency sweeps with single commands.

signals.title: Open Source Radar · 2026-10-26: When another agent is worth opening - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
* Analytics exist, and the boundary is documented. Launches, chat creation, message sends, provider connections and error reports are sent by default, tied to a random installation ID. The README says these exclude prompts, code, files, credentials and account identity; I have not independently audited the telemetry; extra usage sharing is opt-in and `--no-analytics` turns it off for a run.
Compared with: Gentle-AI (entry 3 below) sits at another layer. It only configures agents you already use, and says plainly that it never installs an agent for you and does not own your editor. ThinkRail is the host itself, which is what lets it make the isolation unit a worktree and the protocol its own versioned package. The cost is that its ceiling is set by `pi`'s interface, while the other project buys coverage with 17 agent integrations.
Recent updates: v0.3.0-nightly.6 (2026-10-25) is almost entirely reliability work: terminal recordings persist only after a printed marker arrives, the reading anchor is corrected once after a fold change only once the virtualised list has measured it, and the Windows installer tests warm PowerShell first. Before that, nightly.4 put Remote and Pull request in the topbar with the branch's next step and moved GitHub review details into it; nightly.3 compiled the CLI binary with JSC bytecode and extracted the file and diff renderers into a separate package.
Who it's for: People with several repositories who want to run a few coding agents in parallel, and who can live with a 0.x version and an analytics stream they can switch off. A worktree isolates the working tree only: browser sessions, ports and shared services stay shared. The desktop build is Apple Silicon only on macOS, so Intel machines have to build from source.
My take: ⭐⭐. It treats context as a file-structure problem rather than a prompting problem, which is the part I buy. Too early to be a daily driver.
*Checked: read the README, the last five releases and the last eight commits; not installed.*
### 2. AgriciDaniel/claude-seo ⭐ 21,125 · Python
GitHub: https://github.com/AgriciDaniel/claude-seo
In one line: An SEO audit plugin that runs inside Claude Code, built from 26 sub-skills and 19 specialist agents, up to 17 of them auditing one site in parallel.
What it is: It splits what an SEO consultant checks into skill groups — technical SEO across nine categories, content and E-E-A-T, schema and AI search, local, links and commerce — with 30 commands in six groups hanging off them. A full site audit fans out up to 17 agents and returns Markdown reports that can be turned into PDF. Created 2026-02-07; the five most recent releases, latest v2.5.0 on 2026-10-22.
What stands out:
* Models are assigned by whether a step needs judgement, and the bill is stated. Five of the 19 agents run on Opus (content, AI search, topic clustering, search experience, change monitoring) and the rest on Sonnet. The README says outright that a full audit uses more of your Claude plan than a single-page check, and any agent's model can be changed in `agents/`.
* Findings are intended to include verification steps. Recommendations state what they rest on, what they depend on, and how you will verify them. Reports land as Markdown, PDF and JSON on your machine, and `/seo drift` uses SQLite snapshots to compare audits over time.
* It classifies the business before it checks. SaaS, local, e-commerce, publisher or agency first, then the checklist adapts. JavaScript sites are rendered in a headless browser first, so a single-page app is audited on the rendered DOM, which does not by itself verify every browser interaction or crawler-visible response.
* The CVE check is read-only and does not probe. The server stack CVE exposure check added in v2.5.0 infers the stack from normal response headers (`X-Powered-By`, a PHP session cookie, WordPress signals) according to the release notes: no fuzzing, no exploit payloads, and it asks whether you own the site before requesting any other path.
* The public and paid versions are separate. MIT covers the public plugin; the same author ships a private version to a paid community with earlier access to new features.
Compared with: The project's own FAQ draws the line — crawlers like Screaming Frog crawl faster and deeper, and large SEO suites have their own backlink databases, while this one explains what it finds, sorts by impact, goes deeper on AI search and answers follow-up questions in plain language, and it suggests using both. What is verifiable is the shape of the output: a one-off list versus a repeatable baseline, where every

...

Small tasks run inline with no task document; work only becomes large when it cannot be resumed from the diff — several sessions, external waits, or requirements too long to survive compaction. The feature document of a large task holds your spec verbatim, and every handoff points at it instead of paraphrasing it.
* Eight small components ship with it: a skills library loaded when a task matches, optional Context7 MCP, a read-only CodeGraph symbol map, the security deny-list, config backups before every write, a read-only `gentle-ai doctor`, personas and themes, and per-agent model assignment.
Compared with: It publishes results as a table and puts the caveats next to the table: the author's own local benchmark, hidden acceptance suites, one run per cell (n=1), cost as API-equivalent. A three-line bug in one function went from 335 s, 56 turns and $0.339 to 77 s, 10 turns and $0.105 inline; a bug rooted in shared logic from 479 s and $0.361 to 276 s and $0.207 with one explorer; a 73-line spec with 26 hidden checks failed 13 checks with paraphrased handoffs and was still at 23 of 26 after two feedback rounds, then passed when the spec was passed by reference. The author also compares against the same model in Codex CLI with blind review. The reported large-task duration is 17.5 to 17.9 minutes versus 6.1, a gap the README labels open work. With one run per cell, I would not infer a general acceptance rate or quality ranking. I have not run any of it.
Recent updates: v4.2.0 (2026-10-15) moves Pi's routing block into the provider contract at 1.4.0, byte-identical golden checksums for the other runtimes, and commits work in reviewable slices of about 400 changed lines while keeping small tasks inline. v4.0.0 (2026-10-01) was breaking: the previous methodology retired in favour of ODD, and the module path moved to `/v4`.
Who it's for: Teams with a settled coding agent and a recurring tax of re-explaining the same decisions, and anyone studying explicit review gates. Their effectiveness still depends on the checks and their implementation. Note that it configures rather than installs, that the version is still moving fast, and the trademark notice: MIT covers the code and does not permit implying endorsement.
My take: ⭐⭐⭐. The one I read most closely of these five. It turns two vague questions — when a parallel session is worth opening, and which layer a review should look at — into thresholds, a state machine and a frozen object.
*Checked: read the README and the last five releases; the benchmark table is the project's own claim, not reproduced; not installed.*
### 4. coollabsio/coolify ⭐ 64,540 · PHP
GitHub: https://github.com/coollabsio/coolify
In one line: A self-hosted PaaS that manages servers over SSH alone, deploying applications, databases and more than 360 one-click services, with rollback, backups, patching and an MCP endpoint.
What it is: A Laravel project created 2021-01-25. Sources cover GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket and Gitea; builds run through Nixpacks, Railpack, Dockerfile, Docker Compose or a prebuilt image. The managed unit is a server plus its resources, so multiple servers, container networks, reverse proxies, health checks and certificates all sit in one panel. Latest v4.5.0 on 2026-10-23. The model is free self-hosting plus a paid Cloud; the README's donation section states there is no feature behind the paywall.
* Rollback has two layers, and the second one matches real incidents. One is rollback to a retained application image. Image rollback does not by itself reverse database migrations or external side effects. The new one in v4.5.0 rolls back to a Docker registry image from a recent deployment, which fits the case where CI pushes the image and only environment variables were changed in the panel.
* Patching is treated as a first-class operation. The same release adds server patching in beta: automatic security updates per server, reboot and risky-package warnings, and patch status in the server list.
* It backs itself up before it upgrades. v4.5.0 backs up the Coolify database automatically before an update. A backup is useful only if it can be restored; I have not tested restore coverage or application-data consistency.
* It leaves a door for agents. The same release adds MCP tools to manage resources, alongside a file browser, passkey sign-in, and a Smart scan that detects the build pack, Dockerfiles and environment variables of a new Git project.
* Observability reaches the fleet. A fleet Metrics page has server and container tables, trend charts and one-click enablement; server pages chart disk, network and load; logs can be drained to AWS CloudWatch.
Compared with: Dokploy sits in the same category, and I read both READMEs. The differences that hold up: Coolify leads with a catalogue of more than 360 one-click services, four entry points (panel, API, CLI, MCP) and per-server patching; Dokploy lists multi-node scaling through Docker Swarm and log and metric shipping to a dozen-odd backends including Loki, Prometheus, Datadog and New Relic as first-class features. Both are free to self-host with a paid Cloud, both use Traefik, both run Docker Compose. What is left is the cost of configuration and recovery — how nodes get added, when patch windows land, which backup you restore from — and that has to be measured on your own machines.
Recent updates: v4.5.0 (2026-10-23) lists more than 30 items: Gitea App sources, server patching, fleet Metrics, a Canvas dashboard, file browser, passkeys, maintenance mode and custom error pages, Cloudflare tunnels, a pre-update backup, GitLab system hook deploys, MCP resource management, cache flush for Redis-family databases, and an interactive `docker attach` console. Four patch releases also landed on 2026-10-21, so the release cadence is high.
Who it's for: People with one or a few VPS instances who do not want a Vercel bill or platform lock-in, and small teams needing an internal deployment control plane. Caveats: the panel is itself a single point of failure, and self-hosting means patching and backups remain your responsibility — the tool only hands you the means.
My take: ⭐⭐⭐. Feature density and maintenance activity are both there. The real barrier is not installation but whether you have the operational discipline to use its rollback and patching.
*Checked: read the README and the last five releases, plus Dokploy's README for comparison; no server was deployed.*
### 5. promptfoo/promptfoo ⭐ 26,428 · TypeScript
GitHub: https://github.com/promptfoo/promptfoo
In one line: Treats prompts, agents and RAG systems as code: declarative test cases, automated evals, red-team scanning, side-by-side model comparison and CI integration.
What it is: A TypeScript CLI and library created 2023-04-28. Test cases and assertions are declared in YAML; `promptfoo eval` runs them and `promptfoo view` shows the matrix. Four capability areas: evals, red teaming and vulnerability scanning with generated reports, model comparison across OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure, Bedrock, Ollama and others, and checks inside CI/CD plus pull-request code scanning. Latest 0.125.1 on 2026-10-25.
What stands out:
* The governance changed; the licence did not. The README states at the top that the project is now part of OpenAI and remains open source and MIT licensed; the LICENSE file at the repository root is the standard MIT text.
* It tests assertions, not impressions. 0.125.0 added rouge-l and rouge-s summary assertions and optional Unicode normalisation for equals and contains, which makes text-normalisation policy configurable. Whether normalisation is appropriate depends on the task and the distinctions its assertions need to preserve.
* Repeatability is treated as a metric. The same release reports stability across repeated tests and discloses which rows in the eval summary were cache hits. Without that disclosure, a speedup may just be a cache.
* The safety side has its own switches. 0.125.0 added a safe mode that disables inline JavaScript execution; that setting alone is not a complete sandbox, and made the Claude Agent and Codex SDKs opt-in as a breaking change — it does not connect those runtimes for you by default.
* Comparison is a first-class feature. One set of cases runs against several providers and the matrix lines them up, which is a better answer to "does switching models cost quality" than reading a leaderboard.
Compared with: Together with gentle-ai above, these are the two ends of an evidence chain: one places a change inside a process, the other scores a set of inputs across models. A regression suite earns its place by rerunning: change one prompt and the same cases run again, with results you can compare. What makes this valuable is that cases, assertions, caching and stability become a reusable asset.
One line is easy to misread, so precisely: the README says evals run 100% locally and prompts never leave your machine. The evaluation runner can operate locally; each test request still goes to the configured model endpoint. Check provider, telemetry and optional sharing settings before using sensitive cases.
Recent updates: 0.125.0 (2026-10-23) carries two breaking changes (`jks-js` becomes an optional peer dependency, and the Claude Agent and Codex SDKs become opt-in) plus safe mode, cache-hit disclosure, stability across repeated tests, rouge-l and rouge-s, filtering trace spans by attributes and Unicode normalisation; 0.125.1 (2026-10-25) is a small fix. 0.124.0 (2026-10-06) was a large feature release.

signals.excerpt:
August 25, 2026

# Jalapeño’s first results show industry-leading speed and efficiency in AI inference

Since announcing Jalapeño, OpenAI’s first custom inference chip, we have been testing the chip and the system built around it. The results show a significant performance advance: Jalapeño can serve more AI work per unit of power while also returning responses more quickly. Jalapeño delivers both higher throughput and lower latency with one architecture, where existing hardware systems often have to make a tradeoff between the two.

...

OpenAI models also accelerated Jalapeño’s development. Earlier generations helped the team design and bring up the chip, while our latest models are accelerating how we optimize and program it. Jalapeño’s performance extends across GPT‑OSS 120B, DeepSeek R1, and Kimi K2.5 1T, showing that the architecture works across models developed both inside and outside OpenAI. Across all three, Jalapeño delivered 1.5 to 1.9 times more AI work per watt at peak throughput and 1.7 to 3.6 times lower end-to-end latency than the comparison systems. For highly interactive workloads, it delivered 2.1 to 4.1 times higher performance.

...

We designed Jalapeño to minimize data movement and communication delays. This means that model state, including the KV cache used while generating a response, can be explicitly placed and kept local while the system activates the right combination of compute, memory, and networking for each inference phase. The network is integral to the architecture. Its large domain allows the entire workload to remain within one connected system, minimizing data movement and helping the complete request stay fast and efficient from beginning to end. The result is a balanced and fungible accelerator that can support changing model architectures, excel at both prefill and decode, and adapt as the balance between them changes, a defining feature of agentic workloads.

signals.title: Day 0 support for Mistral Large 4 on vLLM | vLLM Blog
signals.excerpt:
We're excited to announce day-0 support for Mistral Large 4 in vLLM. Mistral Large 4 is Mistral's new frontier mixture-of-experts native multimodal model. It combines a DeepSeek-style sparse attention stack (MLA plus a DSA top-k indexer) with several new architecture features: cross-layer KV sharing, NoPE layers, SSMax and LeRoPE. It ships with a built-in DSpark speculative decoding drafter and a Pixtral vision encoder.

Supporting it took more than a model file. ML4 runs on vLLM's model runner V2 (MRV2) with breakable CUDA graphs. Its building blocks live in a new `vllm/models/mistral/` package, and the work produced generic improvements to decode context parallelism (DCP), prefill context parallelism (PCP), DSpark, NIXL-based disaggregated serving and HiSparse host-memory KV offload.

...

- Architecture: 72-layer MoE with 128 routed experts (top-4) plus 1 shared expert and a hidden size of 6144. Attention is MLA (KV LoRA rank 512, RoPE dim 64) with a DSA sparse indexer that selects the top 2048 keys per query. 1 trillion parameters in total, 49 billion active per token (52 billion including embeddings and output layers).
- Checkpoints: FP8 (block-scaled weights) and NVFP4 (NVFP4 experts, FP8 attention/shared experts). Both use an FP8 latent KV cache (`fp8_ds_mla`) by default.
- Multimodal: a Pixtral vision encoder for image inputs, including multiple images per prompt.
- Speculative decoding: a built-in DSpark drafter (3 sliding-window MLA layers, depth 3) accepts ~2.9 tokens per step and gives about 2x output throughput on TP8.
- Long context: DCP gives ~7.9x more KV capacity on TP8. PCP+DCP prefill cuts time to first token (TTFT) by up to 1.6x. DSpark works under both.
- Disaggregated serving: NIXL prefill/decode (P/D) disaggregation with DP/EP, TP and PCP×DCP prefill nodes, with DSpark on both sides.
- HiSparse: host-memory sparse KV offload, now with support for cross-layer KV sharing.
- AMD: day-0 on AMD Instinct MI350 Series GPUs with ROCm, including DSpark, image inputs and expert parallelism with MXFP4 experts.

...

Mistral Large 4 runs on AMD Instinct MI350 Series GPUs from day 0 with the ROCm build of vLLM. The sparse MLA runs on AITER's MLA decode kernels and the DSA indexer on AITER's gfx950 indexer.

MXFP4 experts. On ROCm the routed experts run as OCP MXFP4 on AITER's fused MoE. There are two ways to get them:

- AMD Quark MXFP4 checkpoint (Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-Quark-MXFP4). Quark re-quantizes only the routed experts, with static weight and dynamic activation scales. Attention, the shared experts, the dense feed-forward layers, the router, the output head, the vision encoder and the DSpark drafter keep their original precision. The checkpoint shrinks from about 1,061 GB to 578 GB, so it serves on four MI350 Series GPUs (288 GB each). The serving commands, evaluation results and the reproduction recipe are on the model card.
- Re-quantize the FP8 checkpoint at load (`VLLM_FP8_MOE_REQUANT=mxfp4`). The experts are converted layer by layer while loading, so peak memory stays low enough for TP4 as well. Expert weights drop from about 125 to 69 GiB per GPU at TP8, and output throughput rises 22–71% over serving the FP8 experts at 1–64 concurrent requests. `VLLM_FP8_MOE_REQUANT_ACT` sets the activation format the MXFP4 experts compute with: `a8w4` (FP8 activations, the default) or `a4w4` (MXFP4 activations).

Either way, one 8-GPU node serves two TP4 replicas, each with about 6× the HBM left for KV cache and activations that the FP8 experts would leave on the same four GPUs.

signals.title: Red Hat ships FP8 and DSpark checkpoints for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL | Batch & Release
signals.excerpt:
# Red Hat ships FP8 and DSpark checkpoints for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL

Red Hat AI releases optimized FP8 and DSpark speculative decoding checkpoints for the 120B multimodal Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, doubling Hopper throughput and cutting memory in half.

Original editorial illustration. Not a product screenshot or measured result.

Red Hat AI has released optimized FP8 and DSpark speculative decoding checkpoints for Open NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120B multimodal mixture-of-experts model designed for long-running agents. The FP8 checkpoints double inference throughput on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs without compromising accuracy, according to Red Hat. FP8 quantization also cuts model weight memory and storage requirements by half compared with BF16, leveraging Hopper's native FP8 Tensor Core support, which provides roughly twice the matrix-multiply throughput of BF16.

## Quantization details

The quantized checkpoints were generated using the LLM Compressor library with a model-free post-training quantization workflow. Quantization is applied to attention, expert, and Mamba projection layers, while shared experts, routers, normalization, and the lm_head remain in BF16. For multi-token prediction layers, attention, expert, and shared expert are quantized, but normalization and the eh_proj layer stay BF16. A creation script in the model card makes the FP8 quantization process fully reproducible.

Red Hat evaluated the FP8 checkpoint on four NVIDIA H200 GPUs using vLLM version 0.31.0, with Inspect AI and Harbor frameworks and non-greedy sampling. The FP8 checkpoint consistently preserves model accuracy across all evaluated benchmarks, the company reports.

...

DSpark speculative decoding drafts 8 to 16 tokens in a single forward pass. It adds a lightweight Markov head to introduce dependencies between speculated tokens, yielding higher-quality candidate sequences and increased inference throughput. Benchmarks on four NVIDIA H100 GPUs used HumanEval, math_reasoning, and RAG datasets.

Replacing the BF16 checkpoint with FP8 primarily boosts aggregate throughput under load. Swapping the MTP speculator for DSpark at BF16 mainly improves single-user streaming speed. Combining FP8 quantization and DSpark outperforms each alone at every concurrency level, according to Red Hat.

## Availability

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL models are available via Red Hat Inference Hub on Red Hat AI Factory with NVIDIA. The optimized checkpoints target inference engineers serving large multimodal models on Hopper hardware, offering a path to higher throughput and lower memory footprint without retraining.

signals.excerpt:
Thu, 29th Oct 2026 (Yesterday) 

 JOSEPH GABRIEL LAGONSIN News Editor 

Google and its partners have released llm-d 1.0, an open-source software stack for distributed large language model inference on Kubernetes. More than 500 contributors from 25 organisations back the project under the Cloud Native Computing Foundation sandbox.

The release formalises a system designed to help companies run AI model-serving workloads across clusters of model servers, rather than on single machines or behind standard load balancers. Co-founded by Google, Red Hat, IBM and other contributors, it links model-serving tools from the PyTorch ecosystem with Kubernetes infrastructure used in production environments.

llm-d 1.0 targets a shift in AI inference traffic from simple one-prompt interactions to multi-step agent workloads and reinforcement learning rollouts. These workloads can arrive in bursts, reuse long prompt prefixes and compete with interactive requests, creating delays and duplicate memory use when traffic is spread inefficiently across servers.

The stack includes routing that tracks where a session's cached context is already stored, a tiered key-value cache system, and flow control designed to separate latency-sensitive requests from background workloads. It can route requests across vLLM and SGLang deployments, as well as mixed fleets of cloud TPUs and GPUs, through a single endpoint.

...

Google cited several benchmark results for the software and related services. In one coding workload on Ironwood TPU, prefix-aware routing and host-memory offload reduced median time-to-first-token by more than 85% and increased total throughput by 2.4 times, compared with a standard Kubernetes Service.

Google also pointed to production use in the Gemini platform, formerly Vertex AI, where GKE Inference Gateway reportedly doubled prefix cache hit rates from 35% to 70%. The company said that change cut time-to-first-token by more than 35% for coding agents and reduced P95 time-to-first-token by more than 50% under bursty chat traffic.

In another published benchmark, Google said a 17,000-node multi-region deployment serving a mixture-of-experts model across the US and Europe increased throughput by 2.9 times across three clusters, with a 99.9% success rate and less than 1% routing overhead. A separate benchmark on an A3 Mega cluster serving a 70 billion-parameter model showed about a 40% improvement in time-to-first-token and a 30% reduction in end-to-end latency for 50,000-token prompts when using multi-connector cache offloading to Managed Lustre in addition to host memory.

Smaller apps and faster GPU inference with LiteRT in Google Play services

signals.excerpt:
LiteRT in Google Play services is Android's on-device inference runtime for custom models, handling more than a trillion inferences a day across billions of devices. Today, it gets its biggest upgrade yet: GPU inference that runs about 1.4x faster than the legacy GPU delegate, powered by ML Drift and available through the new CompiledModel API, LiteRT’s modern successor to the legacy Interpreter API.

Until now, taking advantage of this faster GPU stack required bundling LiteRT in your app. In our testing, apps that switched to LiteRT in Google Play services are about 8 MB smaller, making them faster to download and lighter on users' devices, because the runtime, including the GPU accelerator, ships once with Play services rather than inside every app. More than 100K Android apps bundle their own copy of LiteRT or TensorFlow Lite today, so the savings add up quickly as apps switch.

### CompiledModel API

 LiteRT is the evolution of TensorFlow Lite. It keeps the same .tflite model format you rely on and adds the CompiledModel API, which makes acceleration across fragmented hardware reliable:

- Simpler: one workflow for CPU and GPU acceleration instead of a different delegate and setup path for each accelerator. LiteRT uses OpenCL where available and OpenGL otherwise. If you request both GPU and CPU, it falls back to CPU on devices without a usable GPU.
- Faster: powered by ML Drift, LiteRT's latest, open-source GPU engine already used by Google apps on millions of devices daily. GPU inference runs about 1.4x faster than the legacy TensorFlow Lite GPU delegate.
- Portable: cross-platform support, so the same `.tflite` model runs on Android, iOS, desktop, and web.
- Flexible: the legacy Interpreter API is still supported on CPU, so you can migrate in phases.

signals.title: Artificial Analysis v5 and the benchmarker's dilemma
signals.excerpt: Hacker News: 6 points and 0 comments.

candidates.angle: ViBench 2.0, a new benchmark for evaluating AI agents' ability to build entire software products one feature at a time, moving beyond traditional single-task coding benchmarks.
candidates.audience_pain: Difficulty in reliably evaluating AI agents for complex, real-world software development scenarios.
candidates.why_now: Replit's release of ViBench 2.0 addresses a critical gap in agent evaluation for 'long-horizon' tasks, mimicking real product development.

candidates.angle: Google's open-source llm-d 1.0 stack for distributed LLM inference on Kubernetes, designed to scale model serving workloads across clusters rather than single machines or standard load balancers.
candidates.audience_pain: Struggling to scale LLM inference economically and reliably across diverse hardware environments.
candidates.why_now: New open-source release by Google and partners, formalizing a system for Kubernetes-native distributed inference.

candidates.angle: Red Hat's optimized FP8 and DSpark checkpoints for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120B mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, double inference throughput and halve memory on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs without compromising accuracy.
candidates.audience_pain: High inference costs and memory footprints for large MoE models on high-end GPUs.
candidates.why_now: Red Hat's release of optimized FP8 and DSpark checkpoints offers significant performance gains for a frontier MoE model.

candidates.angle: How Sulci 1.0, an open-source, context-aware semantic cache, reduces LLM API calls and improves application efficiency by understanding query intent, even when words differ.
candidates.audience_pain: High LLM API costs and slow response times due to redundant or semantically similar queries.
candidates.why_now: Sulci 1.0 has reached general availability as an Apache 2.0 open-source solution for LLM apps and AI agents.
candidates.hook_seed: Cut LLM API costs with caching.

candidates.topic: Optimizing MoE Inference on NVIDIA DGX
candidates.angle: Specific techniques like Humming MXFP4 MoE kernels and online FP8 quantization that reduce memory-bound decoding and boost inference performance for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models on NVIDIA DGX Spark.
candidates.audience_pain: Struggling to achieve maximum inference throughput and efficiency for MoE models on NVIDIA's high-performance hardware.
candidates.why_now: NVIDIA's technical blog details new, specific low-level optimizations for MoE inference, showing significant throughput gains.

candidates.angle: A deep dive into Mistral Large 4's novel architectural features (cross-layer KV sharing, NoPE layers, SSMax, LeRoPE) and its optimized integration with vLLM's advanced serving capabilities.
candidates.audience_pain: Understanding the latest innovations in LLM architecture and how they translate to efficient serving and deployment.
candidates.why_now: Mistral Large 4's open-weight release and immediate day-0 support in vLLM highlight its frontier model status and advanced design.

candidates.angle: How PyTorch 2.15's FSDP2 and pipelining gain finer memory and communication control, and faster 4-bit (NVFP4) LLM decoding specifically enhance performance for developers working with large language models, especially on Blackwell GPUs.
candidates.audience_pain: Optimizing distributed training and inference performance for large language models within the PyTorch ecosystem.
candidates.why_now: The PyTorch 2.15 release introduces critical features for improving efficiency and performance in LLM infrastructure.

candidates.angle: Google Play services' LiteRT now offers 1.4x faster GPU inference for custom models on Android, reducing app sizes by 8MB and making mobile AI more efficient and accessible through the new CompiledModel API.
candidates.audience_pain: Developing efficient and performant AI features for mobile apps without significantly increasing app size or complexity.
candidates.why_now: Google's announcement of a major upgrade to LiteRT, making faster GPU inference available via Play services, impacting billions of devices.

candidates.angle: OpenAI's Jalapeño, their first custom inference chip, demonstrating a significant performance advance by delivering both higher throughput and lower latency simultaneously for AI inference workloads.
candidates.audience_pain: The inherent trade-off between inference throughput and latency in existing hardware systems often complicates system design.
candidates.why_now: OpenAI's announcement of the first results from their custom Jalapeño chip signals a major development in AI hardware infrastructure.

candidates.angle: Strategies for understanding and managing the consistent 'voice' (style, tone) and factual reliability ('zombie stats') of LLM outputs, crucial for building trustworthy production applications.
candidates.audience_pain: LLM outputs often lack consistent tone, style, or factual accuracy, leading to untrustworthy user experiences or misleading information.
candidates.why_now: High community engagement around 'LLM Voice' and 'Zombie Stats' on Hacker News signals an ongoing, critical challenge for developers deploying LLMs.
